newsitem.title: FINLAND: Yeltsin, Clinton hit right note at summit start.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Clinton hit right note at summit start.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

The United States and Russia started a difficult summit dominated by NATO enlargement on Thursday, but the two leaders got off to a friendly start and both stressed the value of their post-Cold War partnership.

U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin, at their first meeting in almost a year, struck a positive and jovial note at their initial summit session over dinner on Thursday, their spokesmen said.

With the main summit talks set for Friday, they clearly wanted first to re-establish their warm working relationship and dispel some of the threatening atmopshere that had built up ahead of the summit over Russia's opposition to NATO expansion.
Briefing reporters after the leaders dined on salmon and reindeer with Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari, White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters:
"The president and Yeltsin were clearly striking a tone for the meeting which seemed to be very positive. There was a lot of banter back and forth."

Russian presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky, at a separate briefing, dropped his thunderous warnings about the risks of enlarging NATO and spoke in similar terms about "optimistic realism" and of determination to get results.

"There were lots of jokes, including jokes about health," he said. Clinton is temporarily confined to a wheelchair following surgery for a leg injury and Yeltsin has only recently emerged from months of illness following a heart operation.

McCurry said the two men had not attempted to get into serious negotiations on NATO or other subjects over the dinner. But he quoted Clinton as saying of Yeltsin: "I think he really came here to do business."
Yastrzhembsky, too, said Yeltsin had told him he felt they would be able to tackle their tricky summit agenda, which also covers arms control and Russia's transition to a market economy.
On arrival in the Finnish capital, Yeltsin said he and Clinton faced "difficult, serious talks" but that it was important to find compromises and sustain the relationship.
The 66-year-old Kremlin chief looked well, although stiff and somewhat drawn, clearly still recovering his health.
Yeltsin arrived some three hours after the wheelchair-bound Clinton, who had to be lifted unceremoniously from the presidential jumbo jet in an airport catering truck.
Russia says NATO's expansion plans will threaten its security, undermine Yeltsin, create new divisions in Europe and represent a breach of trust.
An alliance summit in July is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to start membership talks. The new members would not join until 1999 at the earliest.
Earlier, Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin would defend Moscow's interests "like never before" and that NATO enlargement was the West's biggest mistake since the end of the Cold War.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who arrived with Clinton and held preparatory talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, said NATO enlargement would happen on schedule and dismissed Yastrzhembsky's remarks as unimportant "rhetoric".

U.S. officials said they would also press Russia at the summit to ratify within the next few weeks a long-delayed 1993 arms agreement cutting long-range nuclear missiles, perhaps with the help of additional concessions from Washington.

Yeltsin has just reshuffled his government to bring in more reformers but must be seen to fight Russia's corner by his communist and nationalist critics at home. In Moscow, his parliamentary opponents put off until Friday a debate on NATO.

Former Soviet president Mikhail Gorbachev, on a visit to Argentina, warned Clinton on Thursday not to "flex his muscles" over NATO and said enlargement would be "laying a minefield under the whole post-Cold War process".
Clinton and Yeltsin may discuss the latest crisis in the Middle East peace process co-sponsored by Moscow and Washington.

They will also tackle economic questions. There is likely to be more Western help on offer to support Russia as it tackles organised crime and economic reforms, particularly since Yeltsin has pleased Washington by his clear commitment to change.
